title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

questions.title: Defining Economic Scarcity
questions.prompt_template: Which statement best defines the economic condition of scarcity?

hints.text: Think about why even wealthy households and rich nations still face economic trade-offs every day.
Scarcity compares limited productive resources against virtually unlimited human wants.

options_template.text: A temporary market shortage caused by a store running out of a discounted product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage vs. Scarcity): A temporary shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price, whereas scarcity is a permanent condition.

options_template.text: The condition in which limited productive resources cannot simultaneously satisfy all human wants.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Scarcity arises from the collision between finite resources (time, money, land, labor, capital) and limitless wants, forcing choices.

options_template.text: A state of low household income that disappears once a society achieves high average wealth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Poverty vs. Scarcity): Even billionaires face scarce time (24 hours per day) and finite wealth relative to all possible uses.

options_template.text: An artificial restriction created solely when governments impose price controls or taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Only Attribution): Scarcity is a natural physical constraint on resources and exists regardless of government intervention.

questions.title: Precise Definition of Opportunity Cost
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a student has two free hours and ranks three mutually exclusive uses of that time: (1) studying for an economics exam, (2) working a paid campus shift, and (3) taking a nap. If the student chooses to study, what is the opportunity cost of that decision?

hints.text: Opportunity cost measures what you actually give up when you choose one option over the alternatives.
Remember that you could only have done one alternative during those same two hours—not all of them combined.

options_template.text: The value of working the paid campus shift, which is the single next-best alternative forgone.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Opportunity cost is specifically the value of the highest-ranked alternative sacrificed, not the sum of every rejected option.

options_template.text: The combined value of both working the paid campus shift and taking a nap.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Summing All Alternatives): Because the alternatives are mutually exclusive, the student could not have worked and napped at the same time.

options_template.text: Zero, because studying for an exam requires no out-of-pocket cash payment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Explicit-Only Bias): Time has an implicit opportunity cost even when no cash changes hands.

options_template.text: The value of taking a nap, because it is the lowest-ranked alternative on the list.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lowest-Ranked Alternative Error): Opportunity cost is measured by the best forgone option, not the least-valued one.

questions.title: Distinguishing Explicit and Implicit Costs
questions.prompt_template: How do economists distinguish between explicit costs and implicit costs when measuring total economic cost?

hints.text: Think about which costs appear on a receipt or accounting ledger and which reflect forgone opportunities of owned resources.
Total economic cost equals explicit costs plus implicit costs.

options_template.text: Explicit costs occur in the short run, whereas implicit costs occur only in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Time-Horizon Confusion): Both explicit and implicit costs exist in the short run and the long run.

options_template.text: Explicit costs are fixed regardless of output, whereas implicit costs always vary with output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed vs. Variable Confusion): Explicit costs can be fixed (rent) or variable (supplies), and implicit costs represent non-monetary opportunity costs.

options_template.text: Explicit costs are direct out-of-pocket monetary payments, whereas implicit costs are the non-monetary value of forgone time, wages, or alternative uses of owned assets.
options_template.feedback: Correct. True economic opportunity cost combines cash outlays (explicit) with the value of self-owned resources used in the activity (implicit).

options_template.text: Explicit costs are paid by firms, whereas implicit costs are paid exclusively by consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Agent Misclassification): Both households (e.g., college students) and firms (e.g., business owners) incur explicit and implicit costs.

questions.title: Identifying a Sunk Cost
questions.prompt_template: You paid $80 last month for a non-refundable concert ticket. Tonight a severe winter storm makes driving hazardous. According to rational economic decision-making, how should the $80 ticket price affect your choice tonight?

hints.text: Ask yourself whether staying home or driving to the arena changes whether you get the $80 back.
Unrecoverable past spending is a sunk cost and should not enter forward-looking marginal comparisons.

options_template.text: It should be added to tonight's marginal benefit so you do not waste the $80.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk Cost Fallacy): Attending in a blizzard does not recover the $80; it only adds safety risk and lost study time.

options_template.text: It represents your explicit opportunity cost of staying home tonight.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk Cost as Opportunity Cost): Because the $80 is gone under either choice, it is not sacrificed by staying home.

options_template.text: It should be divided by the number of concert hours to determine tonight's marginal cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average Sunk Cost Error): Dividing an unrecoverable historical outlay by hours still measures a sunk cost, not an incremental cost.

options_template.text: It should be ignored because it is an unrecoverable sunk cost regardless of whether you attend or stay home.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rational decisions weigh only future incremental benefits against future opportunity costs (safety and time), ignoring sunk costs.

questions.title: Positive Accounting Profit with an Economic Loss
questions.prompt_template: Under what condition does a small business owner earn a positive accounting profit while simultaneously experiencing an economic loss?

hints.text: Compare the formulas: Accounting Profit = Revenue - Explicit Costs, whereas Economic Profit = Revenue - (Explicit Costs + Implicit Costs).
Think about what happens when revenue covers all cash bills but falls short of covering the owner's forgone salary and interest.

options_template.text: Total revenue exceeds explicit costs, but falls short of the sum of explicit and implicit costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs (such as forgone salary), accounting profit can be positive even when economic profit is negative.

options_template.text: Explicit costs exceed total revenue while implicit costs equal zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Accounting Profit): If explicit costs exceed revenue, both accounting profit and economic profit are negative.

options_template.text: Implicit costs are negative, causing economic cost to fall below explicit cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Implicit Cost): Forgone wages and interest from owned resources are non-negative opportunity costs, so economic cost is at least as large as explicit cost.

options_template.text: Total revenue equals total economic cost while explicit costs are strictly positive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Economic Profit Confusion): When revenue equals total economic cost, economic profit is zero (break-even), not an economic loss.

questions.title: The Marginal Decision Rule
questions.prompt_template: When an activity is chosen in indivisible discrete units (such as whole hours or whole workers), how should a rational decision-maker apply marginal analysis to maximize net benefit?

hints.text: Compare the extra benefit (MB) and extra cost (MC) of each successive unit one at a time.
Keep adding a unit whenever MB >= MC, and stop before taking a unit whose MC exceeds its MB.

options_template.text: Continue expanding the activity until total benefit reaches its absolute maximum, regardless of cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Benefit-Only Maximization): Maximizing total benefit ignores rising costs and pushes the decision into units where MC > MB, reducing net benefit.

options_template.text: Expand as long as a unit's marginal benefit is at least as large as its marginal cost, and stop before the first unit where MC > MB.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Each unit with MB > MC adds to net benefit, while any unit with MC > MB subtracts from net benefit.

options_template.text: Stop at the exact unit where marginal benefit is at its highest level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stopping at Peak MB): Stopping when MB peaks leaves profitable units unchosen whenever subsequent units still have MB > MC.

options_template.text: Expand until average benefit equals average cost so total net benefit is driven to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Value Rule): Setting average benefit equal to average cost equates total benefit to total cost, yielding zero net benefit rather than maximum net benefit.

questions.title: Why Marginal Cost Differs from Average Cost
questions.prompt_template: Why can a firm's marginal cost of serving one additional customer be much lower than its average cost per customer?

hints.text: Review how total fixed costs (such as a scheduled flight's committed operating cost) affect average cost versus marginal cost.
Average cost divides total cost by all units, while marginal cost counts only the extra cost of the next unit.

options_template.text: Because marginal cost always excludes labor and fuel expenses, whereas average cost includes them.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Input Exclusion Error): Marginal cost includes all extra variable inputs (such as extra fuel, snacks, or handling) needed for the additional unit.

options_template.text: Because average cost measures implicit costs only, while marginal cost measures explicit costs only.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Explicit/Implicit Conflation): Both average and marginal economic costs can include explicit and implicit components.

options_template.text: Because average cost spreads already-committed fixed costs across all units, whereas marginal cost isolates only the incremental cost of adding one more unit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When fixed costs are already committed (like a scheduled flight), serving one more unit adds only small variable costs, keeping MC well below AC.

options_template.text: Because marginal cost is always equal to zero once a business opens its doors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-MC Overgeneralization): Incremental units typically still require positive variable resources (fuel, materials, labor), so MC is usually positive.

questions.title: How Incentives Alter Behavior
questions.prompt_template: In microeconomics, how does an incentive change a rational decision-maker's behavior?

hints.text: Connect incentives directly to the two sides of the marginal ledger: marginal benefit (MB) and marginal cost (MC).
Taxes, subsidies, fines, and rewards alter the payoff of taking one more unit of an action.

options_template.text: It eliminates scarcity so individuals no longer face trade-offs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elimination of Scarcity): Incentives alter the relative costs and benefits of choices, but resources remain finite.

options_template.text: It forces every individual to make the exact same choice regardless of preferences.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform-Outcome Assumption): People respond predictably in direction at the margin, but individual choices still vary with personal preferences and circumstances.

options_template.text: It operates only through monetary cash bonuses and cannot involve non-monetary penalties or risks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cash-Only Incentive View): Incentives include non-monetary factors such as safety risk, time delays, social norms, and legal penalties.

options_template.text: It acts as a reward or penalty that shifts marginal benefit (MB) or marginal cost (MC), prompting predictable adjustments at the margin.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Changing MB or MC alters which units satisfy MB >= MC, leading rational agents to expand or contract the activity.

questions.title: The Role of Simplifying Assumptions in Economic Models
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists deliberately omit many real-world details—much like a subway map omits trees and storefronts—when constructing an economic model?

hints.text: Think about what makes a map useful for navigating a city rather than recreating every blade of grass.
Models strip away secondary noise so analysts can isolate specific cause-and-effect relationships.

options_template.text: To strip away secondary noise and isolate how one specific variable affects another clearly.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Useful economic models are intentionally simplified analytical maps designed to highlight key mechanisms and testable predictions.

options_template.text: Because economic data are impossible to collect in modern economies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Data-Absence Myth): Economists routinely use vast empirical datasets; simplification is an analytical choice to focus on core relationships.

options_template.text: To guarantee that every model's predictions are 100% exact in every real-world situation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfection Fallacy): Simplifying assumptions clarify core trade-offs and predictions, which must still be tested against empirical evidence.

options_template.text: Because microeconomic models cannot include more than one mathematical variable.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Variable Myth): Economic models frequently include multiple variables (such as R = 120 - 15F + 10G) while holding secondary factors constant.

questions.title: Purpose of the Ceteris Paribus Assumption
questions.prompt_template: When an economist states that a lower coffee price increases the quantity of coffee demanded, ceteris paribus, what does the phrase ceteris paribus mean?

hints.text: Recall the literal Latin translation introduced in Section 1.3.
This assumption freezes confounding determinants—such as income, weather, and competitor prices—so one effect can be isolated.

options_template.text: The price cut is guaranteed to be socially desirable for consumers and cafes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normative Conflation): Ceteris paribus is a methodological assumption about holding variables constant, not a value judgment.

options_template.text: All other relevant factors—such as consumer income, weather, tastes, and competitor prices—are held constant.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Holding other determinants fixed lets economists isolate the pure relationship between coffee price and quantity demanded.

options_template.text: All variables in the economy change proportionally at the exact same rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Proportional-Change Inversion): Ceteris paribus holds non-focal factors fixed rather than varying them together.

options_template.text: The relationship holds only in the absence of government taxes or regulations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Laissez-Faire Confusion): Ceteris paribus simply holds existing policies and outside factors unchanged while analyzing one variable's effect.

questions.title: Positive Statements Need Not Be Factually True
questions.prompt_template: Consider the claim: 'Raising college tuition always increases total student enrollment.' How should an economist classify this statement?

hints.text: Distinguish between whether a claim is testable against data versus whether it is factually accurate or expresses a value judgment.
A statement about what is or what happens—even if empirically wrong—differs from a 'should' or 'ought' statement.

options_template.text: Normative, because the claim is almost certainly false in real-world data.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (False-Equals-Normative): Being factually incorrect does not make a statement normative; testability, not truth, defines positive claims.

options_template.text: Normative, because college tuition is an emotionally debated public policy topic.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Topic-Based Classification): Any policy topic can be discussed using either positive (testable) or normative (value-laden) statements.

options_template.text: Positive, because it makes a testable claim about how the world works that can be checked and refuted with evidence.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive economics encompasses testable statements about what is or what happens; a false positive claim is still positive because data can falsify it.

options_template.text: Neither positive nor normative, because economists only study statements that are proven true.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unproven Exclusion): Testing and refuting hypotheses is the core of positive empirical economics.

questions.title: Omitted Variable Bias and Spurious Correlation
questions.prompt_template: City health data show that monthly ice cream sales and monthly swimming accidents rise and fall together throughout the year. What methodological error occurs if an analyst concludes that eating ice cream causes swimming accidents?

hints.text: Ask whether a third seasonal variable could be driving both ice cream consumption and swimming activity.
Observing two variables move together does not establish a direct causal link.

options_template.text: The sunk cost fallacy, because past ice cream spending cannot be recovered.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misnamed Fallacy): Sunk cost fallacy involves unrecoverable historical outlays, not mistaking association for causation.

options_template.text: The average cost fallacy, because monthly totals should be divided by population.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Concept Mismatch): Per-capita scaling does not solve an omitted third variable driving both series.

options_template.text: A normative value judgment, because swimming safety involves ethical priorities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Positive/Normative Mismatch): Claiming ice cream causes accidents is a flawed positive causal claim, not an ethical 'ought' statement.

options_template.text: Confusing correlation with causation by ignoring an omitted third variable (warm summer weather) that drives both.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Correlation does not prove causation; warm weather independently increases both ice cream purchases and swimming frequency.

questions.title: Separating Microeconomic and Macroeconomic Questions
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following questions falls squarely within microeconomics rather than macroeconomics?

hints.text: Microeconomics zooms in on individual markets, households, and firms; macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates.
Look for the question centered on a specific local market price or individual firm/household behavior.

options_template.text: How does a city's zoning reform affect apartment rents and landlord construction incentives in San Francisco?
options_template.feedback: Correct. Analyzing prices, rents, and incentives within a specific local market is a classic microeconomic inquiry.

options_template.text: How does a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike affect national real GDP growth next year?
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro Aggregate Scope): National GDP growth and central-bank monetary policy are macroeconomic topics.

options_template.text: Why did the U.S. national unemployment rate rise during the most recent recession?
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro Labor Aggregate): Economy-wide unemployment across the entire nation is studied in macroeconomics.

options_template.text: How do changes in federal fiscal deficits affect the economy-wide inflation rate?
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro Fiscal/Inflation Scope): National fiscal deficits and aggregate inflation belong to macroeconomics.

questions.title: Reading Axis Intercepts on a Linear Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.1, a student's weekly budget line is 12X + 6Y = 60, where X is campus lunches ($12 each) on the horizontal axis and Y is transit day-passes ($6 each) on the vertical axis. What do the vertical intercept (0, 10) and horizontal intercept (5, 0) represent?

hints.text: Set X = 0 to find the vertical intercept and set Y = 0 to find the horizontal intercept.
Each intercept shows the maximum quantity of one good affordable if the entire $60 budget is spent on that good alone.

options_template.text: The unit prices of transit passes ($10) and campus lunches ($5).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Intercept Confusion): Prices are $12 and $6; the intercepts are quantities (I/Py = 10 and I/Px = 5), not prices.

options_template.text: The maximum quantities affordable when spending the entire $60 exclusively on transit passes (10 passes) or exclusively on lunches (5 lunches).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At (0, 10), $60 buys 60/6 = 10 passes and 0 lunches; at (5, 0), $60 buys 60/12 = 5 lunches and 0 passes.

options_template.text: The student's two most preferred bundles regardless of income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Preference vs. Feasibility): A budget line shows what is affordable, not which bundle maximizes satisfaction.

options_template.text: The total dollar expenditure on transit passes ($10) and lunches ($5) at equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-Quantity Swap): Axes measure physical quantities of goods X and Y, not dollar totals.

questions.title: Interpreting the Slope of a Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: Along the linear budget line 12X + 6Y = 60 (rewritten as Y = 10 - 2X), moving from bundle A(2, 6) to bundle B(3, 4) illustrates which graphical property?

hints.text: Calculate the rise over run: Delta Y / Delta X = (4 - 6) / (3 - 2).
Because the budget line is straight, its slope magnitude |Delta Y / Delta X| = Px / Py is constant everywhere along the line.

options_template.text: Increasing opportunity cost, because each extra lunch requires giving up more passes than the last.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curved-PPF Confusion): A straight budget line has a constant slope (-2), representing constant—not increasing—opportunity cost.

options_template.text: An outward shift of the budget constraint caused by higher weekly income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): Moving from A to B stays on the same line with fixed income ($60) and fixed prices.

options_template.text: A constant slope of -2, meaning gaining 1 additional campus lunch requires sacrificing exactly 2 transit day-passes.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The slope -Px/Py = -12/6 = -2 shows a constant trade-off of 2 transit passes per campus lunch.

options_template.text: A constant opportunity cost of 0.5 transit day-passes per campus lunch.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Slope Error): Computing Delta X / Delta Y = 1/2 = 0.5 gives the opportunity cost of 1 transit pass in lunches, not 1 lunch in passes.

questions.title: Classifying Points Inside, On, and Outside the Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: On the weekly budget diagram for 12X + 6Y = 60, point A(2, 6) lies on the line, point C(2, 4) lies strictly inside (below) the line, and point U(4, 6) lies outside (above) the line. How are these three bundles classified?

hints.text: Compute the cost 12X + 6Y for each bundle and compare it to the $60 budget.
Points on the line exhaust the budget, points inside leave unspent cash, and points outside exceed $60.

options_template.text: Only point U(4, 6) is affordable because it contains more of both goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Desirability vs. Feasibility): U(4, 6) costs 12(4) + 6(6) = $84 > $60, making it unaffordable under the current budget.

options_template.text: Point C(2, 4) is unaffordable because it does not lie on the budget line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interior-Point Misreading): C(2, 4) costs 12(2) + 6(4) = $48 < $60, so it is affordable with $12 left unspent.

options_template.text: All three bundles cost exactly $60 because they appear on the same coordinate plane.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Coordinate-Plane Misreading): Only points directly on the line satisfy 12X + 6Y = 60.

options_template.text: A(2, 6) exhausts the $60 budget, C(2, 4) is affordable with $12 unspent, and U(4, 6) is unaffordable at $84.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A costs $60 (on the boundary), C costs $48 (inside the budget set), and U costs $84 (outside the budget set).

questions.title: Effect of an Income Increase on the Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: Starting from the budget line 12X + 6Y = 60, suppose the student's weekly budget rises from $60 to $72 while the prices of lunches ($12) and transit passes ($6) remain unchanged. How does the budget line move?

hints.text: Check both intercepts (I/Py and I/Px) and the slope (-Px/Py) before and after income increases.
When income rises and prices are unchanged, both intercepts increase while the price ratio stays the same.

options_template.text: It shifts outward in a parallel fashion: the horizontal intercept moves from 5 to 6, the vertical intercept moves from 10 to 12, and the slope stays -2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher income with fixed prices expands both intercepts proportionally (72/12 = 6; 72/6 = 12) without changing the slope -Px/Py = -2.

options_template.text: It pivots outward around the vertical intercept (0, 10) while becoming flatter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Cut Pivot Confusion): A pivot around one intercept happens when only one good's price changes, not when income rises.

options_template.text: It shifts inward toward the origin because higher income raises the opportunity cost of lunches.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): More income expands the affordable set outward and leaves the price ratio Px/Py unchanged.

options_template.text: It becomes steeper with a slope of -3 while keeping the same intercepts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Income Conflation): Slope depends solely on the relative price ratio -Px/Py, which did not change.

questions.title: Effect of a Price Cut on the Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: Starting from 12X + 6Y = 60, suppose a campus meal discount lowers the price of lunches (X) from $12 to $10 while the transit pass price ($6) and weekly budget ($60) stay fixed. How does the budget line change visually?

hints.text: Check whether the maximum number of transit passes (Y-intercept) changes when only Px falls.
Compute the new horizontal intercept (60/10) and compare the new slope magnitude (10/6) to the old one (12/6).

options_template.text: Both intercepts increase in a parallel shift because the student feels richer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parallel-Shift Error): Because Py and I are unchanged, the vertical intercept remains fixed at 60/6 = 10 transit passes.

options_template.text: It pivots outward along the horizontal axis from X = 5 to X = 6 while staying anchored at Y = 10, making the line flatter.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lowering Px increases the X-intercept to 60/10 = 6, leaves the Y-intercept at 10, and reduces the slope magnitude from 2 to 10/6 = 1.67.

options_template.text: It pivots inward along the horizontal axis from X = 5 to X = 4, making the line steeper.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Inversion): A lower price allows buying more lunches, rotating the X-intercept outward rather than inward.

options_template.text: It pivots upward along the vertical axis from Y = 10 to Y = 12 while staying anchored at X = 5.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Axis Rotation): Changing Px rotates the X-axis intercept (horizontal axis), not the Y-axis intercept.

questions.title: Interpreting Points to the Left of the MB = MC Intersection
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.2 (MB = 20 - 3H and MC = 2H, intersecting at H* = 4 hours and $8/hr), a vertical teal arrow at H = 2 shows MB = $14/hr lying above MC = $4/hr. What does this vertical gap indicate?

hints.text: Compare the height of the MB curve to the height of the MC curve at H = 2.
Whenever MB lies above MC, expanding the activity adds more to total benefit than to total cost.

options_template.text: The student is over-studying and should cut back below 2 hours to save cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Region Reversal): Over-studying occurs to the right of H* = 4 where MC > MB, not to the left where MB > MC.

options_template.text: Net benefit is maximized at H = 2 because the vertical gap between MB and MC is large.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Max-Gap Fallacy): Maximizing the marginal gap MB - MC is not maximizing total net benefit; every additional hour from 2 to 4 still adds positive net benefit.

options_template.text: The student is under-studying: increasing study time beyond 2 hours adds positive net benefit because MB ($14/hr) exceeds MC ($4/hr).
options_template.feedback: Correct. To the left of H* = 4, MB > MC, so adding study hours increases total net benefit until H* = 4.

options_template.text: Total benefit equals $14 and total cost equals $4 at H = 2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Marginal-as-Total Reading): Curve heights on a marginal graph show marginal rates ($/hr) at H = 2, not cumulative totals.

questions.title: Interpreting Points to the Right of the MB = MC Intersection
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.2 (MB = 20 - 3H and MC = 2H, intersecting at H* = 4), suppose a student studies H = 5 hours, where the MC curve ($10/hr) lies above the MB curve ($5/hr). What happens to total net benefit if the student cuts back from 5 hours toward 4 hours?

hints.text: Ask whether the fifth hour added more cost or more benefit.
Eliminating an hour where MC > MB saves more cost than the benefit it sacrifices.

options_template.text: Total net benefit falls because studying fewer hours always lowers total benefit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Benefit-Only Focus): Although total benefit declines slightly, total cost declines by even more between H = 5 and H = 4.

options_template.text: Total net benefit is unchanged because both curves are linear.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linearity Misinterpretation): Linear marginal curves produce a quadratic net benefit curve with a unique peak at H* = 4.

options_template.text: Total net benefit becomes negative unless the student studies until MB = 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MB = 0 Fallacy): Studying until MB = 0 ignores rising marginal costs and reduces net benefit below its peak.

options_template.text: Total net benefit increases because cutting back eliminates an hour whose marginal cost exceeds its marginal benefit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. To the right of H* = 4, MC > MB, so reducing hours back toward H* = 4 raises total net benefit.

questions.title: Comparative Statics: Upward Shift in Marginal Benefit
questions.prompt_template: Starting from Figure 1.2's equilibrium at H* = 4 hours and $8/hr, suppose the instructor doubles the exam's weight in the course grade, shifting the student's Marginal Benefit (MB) curve upward while the Marginal Cost (MC) curve stays unchanged. How does the optimal choice E* move?

hints.text: Shift the downward-sloping MB line upward while keeping the upward-sloping MC line fixed.
Trace the new intersection along the fixed upward-sloping MC curve.

options_template.text: The intersection moves up and to the right along MC: optimal study hours H* increase and equilibrium MB = MC rises above $8/hr.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shifting MB upward against an upward-sloping MC moves the optimum right (higher H*) and up (higher equilibrium marginal value).

options_template.text: The intersection moves down and to the left along MC: optimal study hours H* decrease.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Direction Reversal): A higher exam weight raises the marginal payoff of each study hour, encouraging more—not fewer—hours.

options_template.text: Optimal study hours H* increase, while equilibrium MB = MC falls below $8/hr.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Downward-MC Assumption): Because MC slopes upward, moving to a higher H* along MC requires a higher marginal cost at the new optimum.

options_template.text: Optimal study hours H* stay fixed at 4 because MC did not shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (One-Curve-Only Inertia): Any shift in either MB or MC alters the MB = MC intersection.

questions.title: Comparative Statics: Upward Shift in Marginal Cost
questions.prompt_template: Starting from Figure 1.2 (H* = 4 hours, $8/hr), suppose the student's campus job offers an overtime pay bonus on the night before the exam, shifting the Marginal Cost (MC) of studying upward at every hour while MB stays unchanged. How does the optimal study choice change?

hints.text: A higher overtime wage increases the opportunity cost (MC) of each hour spent studying.
Shift the upward-sloping MC curve upward/left along the fixed downward-sloping MB curve.

options_template.text: Both optimal study hours H* and equilibrium marginal value increase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MB-Shift Confusion): Higher MC shifts the intersection up and to the left along MB, reducing H*.

options_template.text: Optimal study hours H* decrease below 4, while the equilibrium marginal value MB = MC rises above $8/hr.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shifting MC upward moves the intersection up and left along the downward-sloping MB curve: fewer study hours, higher marginal value at the last hour studied.

options_template.text: Both optimal study hours H* and equilibrium marginal value decrease.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Upward-MB Assumption): Moving left along a downward-sloping MB curve raises—rather than lowers—the marginal benefit of the last hour kept.

options_template.text: The MB curve shifts downward while MC stays fixed, leaving equilibrium value unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Curve Shift): A higher outside wage raises the opportunity cost of studying (MC), rather than changing the exam payoff of studying (MB).

questions.title: Geometric Area Representing Maximum Total Net Benefit
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.2 (MB = 20 - 3H, MC = 2H, intersecting at H* = 4 and $8/hr), which geometric region on the graph equals the student's maximum total net benefit ($40)?

hints.text: Remember that total benefit is the area under MB from 0 to H*, and total cost is the area under MC from 0 to H*.
Subtract the area under MC from the area under MB between H = 0 and H* = 4.

options_template.text: The rectangle formed by the origin, H* = 4, and $8/hr (area = $32).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rectangle Formula Error): Multiplying equilibrium value by H* ignores the higher MB on earlier hours and the lower MC on earlier hours.

options_template.text: The triangle underneath the MC curve from H = 0 to H* = 4 (area = $16).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Cost Area Confusion): The triangle below MC equals Total Cost ($16), not Net Benefit ($40).

options_template.text: The triangle bounded on the left by the vertical axis (from $0 to $20), above by the MB curve, and below by the MC curve up to H* = 4.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Net benefit equals area under MB ($56) minus area under MC ($16), which is the triangle between MB and MC from 0 to 4: 0.5 * $20 * 4 = $40.

options_template.text: The entire triangle under the MB curve from H = 0 to its horizontal intercept H = 6.67.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring MC Area): The full area under MB ignores total cost entirely and includes hours past H* = 4 where MC > MB.

questions.title: Tracing Outer Clockwise Dollar Flows in the Circular Flow Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.3 (the two-sector Circular Flow Model), what do the solid outer clockwise arrows represent as dollars move around the economy?

hints.text: Trace the solid outer loop starting at Households -> Product Markets -> Firms -> Factor Markets -> Households.
Dollars flow from households as spending into product markets (becoming firm revenue) and from firms as factor payments into factor markets (becoming household income).

options_template.text: Physical goods moving from households to firms and labor services moving from firms to households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow-Type & Role Reversal): Physical flows are on the inner counter-clockwise loop, and firms produce goods while households supply labor.

options_template.text: Tax payments from households to the government and transfer payments back to households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Out-of-Model Sector): Figure 1.3 is a simplified two-sector model that intentionally abstracts away from government.

options_template.text: Firms spending money in product markets to buy goods from households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer/Seller Swap): In product markets, households are the buyers (spending) and firms are the sellers (earning revenue).

options_template.text: Household spending becoming firm revenue in product markets, and firm factor payments becoming household income in factor markets.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The solid clockwise loop tracks dollar flows: Spending -> Revenue on top, and Factor Payments -> Income on the bottom.

questions.title: Tracing Inner Counter-Clockwise Real Flows in the Circular Flow Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1.3's Circular Flow Diagram, how do households and firms interact in the Factor Markets along the dashed inner counter-clockwise loop?

hints.text: Look at the bottom box (Factor Markets: Land, Labor, Capital, Entrepreneurship) and follow the dashed teal arrows.
Who owns productive resources in the circular flow, and who hires them to produce output?

options_template.text: Households supply productive inputs (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) to factor markets, which flow to firms as factor services.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Households are the resource owners who supply inputs through factor markets to firms, which use those factor services to produce goods and services.

options_template.text: Firms supply physical goods and services to factor markets, which flow to households as consumer goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Product-Market Confusion): Physical goods and services flow from firms to households through Product Markets (top), not Factor Markets (bottom).

options_template.text: Firms supply labor and land to factor markets so households can earn revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Agent-Role Reversal): In the circular flow model, households own and supply the factors of production; firms hire them.

options_template.text: Households pay wages and rent to factor markets in exchange for finished products.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-vs-Real Flow Swap): Wages and rent are dollar payments made by firms (not households) along the outer clockwise loop.

questions.title: Movement Along vs. Shift in the Transit Ridership Model
questions.prompt_template: Consider the transit ridership model R = 120 - 15F + 10G plotted with subway fare F on the horizontal axis and ridership R on the vertical axis (holding gas price G fixed at $4.00 so R = 160 - 15F). How do a higher subway fare F and a higher gasoline price G differ graphically?

hints.text: Distinguish between changing the variable plotted on the horizontal axis (F) versus changing the held-constant determinant (G).
Changing F moves along the existing line; changing G alters the intercept a = 120 + 10G and shifts the whole line.

options_template.text: Both a higher fare F and a higher gas price G shift the entire ridership line upward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-Changes-Shift Error): Changing the axis variable F causes a movement along the fixed line, not a shift of the line.

options_template.text: A higher fare F causes a downward movement along the line R = 160 - 15F, whereas a higher gas price G shifts the entire line upward with the same slope (-15).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Varying F moves along the plotted line (slope -15), while a higher G increases the intercept a = 120 + 10G, shifting the entire line upward in parallel.

options_template.text: A higher fare F shifts the line downward, whereas a higher gas price G causes a movement along the line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift/Movement Inversion): The variable on the axis (F) drives movement along the curve; the outside variable (G) shifts the curve.

options_template.text: A higher gas price G rotates the slope from -15 to -5 while leaving the vertical intercept fixed at 160.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Intercept Confusion): In an additive linear model, changing G changes the vertical intercept (120 + 10G) without altering the fare slope (-15).

questions.title: Opportunity Cost and Remaining Bundle on a Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: A student has a fixed weekly budget of $72 to spend completely on campus meals ($12 each, Good X) and bus passes ($4 each, Good Y). What is the opportunity cost of 1 campus meal in terms of bus passes, and if the student buys 4 campus meals, how many bus passes can they afford?

hints.text: Use Opportunity Cost of 1 X = Px / Py to find the trade-off per meal.
Subtract spending on 4 meals (4 * $12) from $72, then divide the remaining dollars by $4 per bus pass.

options_template.text: Opportunity cost = 3 bus passes; affordable bus passes = 18.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Error): 18 = $72/$4 is the maximum bus passes when buying 0 meals; spending $48 on 4 meals leaves only $24 for bus passes.

options_template.text: Opportunity cost = 4 bus passes; affordable bus passes = 6.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-as-Opportunity-Cost Error): $4 is the dollar price of a bus pass (Py), not the price ratio Px/Py = 12/4 = 3.

options_template.text: Opportunity cost = 3 bus passes; affordable bus passes = 6.
options_template.feedback: Correct. OC of 1 meal = $12/$4 = 3 bus passes. Buying 4 meals costs 4($12) = $48, leaving $72 - $48 = $24, which buys $24/$4 = 6 bus passes.

options_template.text: Opportunity cost = 12 bus passes; affordable bus passes = 12.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-Price Conflation): $12 is the dollar price of a meal, not the ratio Px/Py, and 4 meals leave $24 (6 passes), not $48.

questions.title: Terminating-Decimal Opportunity Cost on a Linear Budget Line
questions.prompt_template: A moviegoer allocates a monthly entertainment budget of $90 between theater tickets ($15 each, Good X) and digital movie rentals ($6 each, Good Y), satisfying 15X + 6Y = 90. What is the constant opportunity cost of 1 theater ticket in terms of digital rentals?

hints.text: Rearrange 15X + 6Y = 90 into slope-intercept form Y = (90/6) - (15/6)X.
The opportunity cost of 1 unit of Good X is the price ratio Px / Py.

options_template.text: 2.5 digital rentals.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Opportunity Cost of 1 X = Px / Py = $15 / $6 = 2.5 digital rentals per theater ticket.

options_template.text: 0.4 digital rentals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Price Ratio): $6 / $15 = 0.4 is the opportunity cost of 1 digital rental in theater tickets, not 1 theater ticket in rentals.

options_template.text: 9.0 digital rentals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Difference Error): Subtracting $15 - $6 = $9 gives the dollar price difference, not the trade-off ratio Px / Py.

options_template.text: 6.0 digital rentals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Confusion): $90 / $15 = 6 is the maximum number of theater tickets affordable, not the opportunity cost per ticket.

questions.title: Four-Year Economic Cost of a College Degree
questions.prompt_template: Suppose attending a public university full-time requires $12,500 per year in tuition, fees, and textbooks, plus $14,000 per year for room and board (which the student would also pay if working full-time). Instead of enrolling, the student could work full-time earning $36,000 per year. Assuming these figures stay constant for 4 years, what is the student's 4-year total economic opportunity cost of attending college?

hints.text: Exclude expenses that would be paid identically under both choices (room and board).
Add annual explicit college-specific costs ($12,500) to annual forgone wages ($36,000), then multiply by 4 years.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Explicit-Only Cost): $12,500 * 4 = $50,000 ignores the $36,000/year in forgone full-time wages.
Correct. Annual economic cost = $12,500 (explicit) + $36,000 (implicit forgone wages) = $48,500/year; over 4 years, 4 * $48,500 = $194,000 (unchanged room and board are excluded).
Diagnostic fallacy (Including Non-Incremental Living Costs): ($12,500 + $14,000 + $36,000) * 4 = $250,000 wrongly counts room and board that would be paid even while working.
Diagnostic fallacy (Implicit-Only Cost): $36,000 * 4 = $144,000 counts forgone wages but omits $50,000 in explicit tuition, fees, and textbooks.

questions.title: Computing Year-1 Economic Profit for an Independent Studio
questions.prompt_template: Elena leaves a salaried job paying $72,000 per year to open a consulting studio. In Year 1, she pays $20,000 for rent, $8,000 for software, and $12,000 for supplies. She also moves $30,000 out of a savings account earning 4% annual interest to hold as refundable office deposits and working capital (recovered if she closes). If Year-1 revenue is $95,000, what is Elena's Year-1 economic profit?

hints.text: Compute Explicit Costs ($20,000 + $8,000 + $12,000) and Implicit Costs ($72,000 salary + 4% forgone interest on $30,000).
Because the $30,000 working-capital deposit is recoverable, include only its $1,200 forgone interest—not the $30,000 principal—in economic cost.

options_template.text: +$55,000 (an economic profit of $55,000).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Profit Substitution): $95,000 - $40,000 = +$55,000 is accounting profit because it omits $73,200 in implicit opportunity costs.

options_template.text: -$17,000 (an economic loss of $17,000).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Forgone Interest): $95,000 - ($40,000 + $72,000) = -$17,000 omits the $1,200 forgone interest (0.04 * $30,000) on Elena's savings.

options_template.text: -$48,200 (an economic loss of $48,200).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Recoverable Principal): Subtracting the $30,000 refundable deposit as a consumed Year-1 expense overstates economic cost by $30,000.

options_template.text: -$18,200 (an economic loss of $18,200).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Explicit = $40,000; Implicit = $72,000 + ($30,000 * 0.04) = $73,200; Total Economic Cost = $113,200; Economic Profit = $95,000 - $113,200 = -$18,200.

questions.title: Minimum Revenue Needed to Cover Full Economic Cost
questions.prompt_template: An entrepreneur expects Year-1 explicit operating costs of $45,000, gives up a $60,000 salaried position, and ties up $25,000 of personal savings (previously earning 6% annual interest) as a refundable lease deposit. What is the minimum Year-1 revenue required to earn zero economic profit?

hints.text: Zero economic profit occurs when Total Revenue equals Explicit Costs plus Implicit Costs.
Calculate the forgone annual interest as $25,000 * 0.06 and add it to the forgone salary and explicit costs.

options_template.feedback: Correct. Forgone interest = $25,000 * 0.06 = $1,500; Total Economic Cost = $45,000 + $60,000 + $1,500 = $106,500.
Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting Break-Even Confusion): $45,000 covers only explicit cash bills, leaving an economic loss of -$61,500.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Capital Opportunity Cost): $45,000 + $60,000 = $105,000 omits the $1,500 forgone interest on the $25,000 deposit.
Diagnostic fallacy (Counting Recoverable Principal as Cost): Adding the $25,000 refundable deposit principal treats a recoverable asset as a Year-1 expense.

questions.title: Solving Linear MB = MC for Optimal Hours
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a student's continuous marginal benefit and marginal cost of studying H hours (measured in $/hr) are given by MB = 30 - 4H and MC = 2H. What is the optimal study time H* and the common value of MB and MC at the optimum?

hints.text: Set the interior optimality condition MB = MC: 30 - 4H = 2H.
Combine the H terms on one side to solve for H*, then substitute H* back into MC = 2H.

options_template.text: H* = 7.5 hours; MB = MC = $0/hr.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Marginal Cost): Setting MB = 0 gives 30 - 4H = 0 => H = 7.5, where MC = $15/hr far exceeds MB.

options_template.text: H* = 5 hours; MB = MC = $10/hr.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 30 - 4H = 2H yields 6H = 30 => H* = 5 hours, where MB = 30 - 4(5) = $10/hr and MC = 2(5) = $10/hr.

options_template.text: H* = 15 hours; MB = MC = $30/hr.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted MB Slope): Dividing 30 by 2 ignores the -4H slope term in the marginal benefit equation.

options_template.text: H* = 6 hours; MB = MC = $12/hr.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Algebraic Combining Error): Adding slopes incorrectly as 4 + 1 = 5 instead of 4 + 2 = 6 yields H = 30/5 = 6, where MB ($6) < MC ($12).

questions.title: Choosing Optimal Indivisible Operating Hours
questions.prompt_template: A neighborhood coffee shop considers staying open up to 5 extra evening hours. The marginal benefit (extra revenue) for hours 1 through 5 is $48, $36, $28, $18, and $10, respectively. The marginal cost (extra staffing and utilities) for hours 1 through 5 is $20, $22, $25, $29, and $35, respectively. How many extra hours should the shop stay open, and what is the resulting total net gain?

hints.text: Compare MB against MC hour by hour: keep an hour only if MB >= MC.
Sum (MB - MC) across all chosen hours to compute the total net gain.

options_template.text: 2 extra hours, yielding a total net gain of $42.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stopping Too Early): Hour 3 still has MB ($28) > MC ($25), so stopping at 2 hours leaves $3 of extra profit on the table.

options_template.text: 4 extra hours, yielding a total net gain of $34.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Expanding Past MB = MC): Hour 4 has MB ($18) < MC ($29), which subtracts $11 from net profit.

options_template.text: 3 extra hours, yielding a total net gain of $45.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Hours 1, 2, and 3 each satisfy MB > MC (net gains of +$28, +$14, and +$3, totaling $45), while Hour 4 has MB ($18) < MC ($29).

options_template.text: 5 extra hours, yielding a total net gain of $9.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Fallacy): Staying open whenever MB > 0 ignores that Hours 4 and 5 lose $11 and $25 respectively.

questions.title: Standby Airline Seat Profit Decision
questions.prompt_template: An airline operates a 180-seat flight whose total committed flight and crew cost is $21,600 (an average cost of $120 per seat). With 15 seats empty just before departure, boarding one standby passenger adds $22 in incremental fuel, snacks, and baggage handling. If a standby passenger offers $85 (and does not displace any full-fare buyer), what is the net change in the airline's profit from selling the seat?

hints.text: Treat the $21,600 flight cost as already committed (sunk) and compare only the standby fare (MB) to the incremental passenger cost (MC).
Compute Net Operating Gain = MB - MC.

options_template.text: -$35 (a loss of $35), so the airline should refuse the offer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Cost Fallacy): Comparing $85 to the $120 average cost wrongly treats already-committed flight costs as avoidable.

options_template.text: -$57 (a loss of $57), because the fare must cover both average cost and marginal cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Fixed and Marginal Cost): Subtracting $120 + $22 = $142 from $85 wrongly treats sunk flight costs as incremental.

options_template.text: +$85 (a gain of $85), because the plane is already flying for free.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Variable Marginal Cost): Even though flight fixed costs are sunk, the airline still incurs $22 in extra variable cost for the standby passenger.

options_template.text: +$63 (a gain of $63), so the airline should sell the seat.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because MB ($85) > MC ($22), selling the standby seat increases profit by $85 - $22 = +$63 regardless of the $120 average cost.

questions.title: Computing Maximum Net Benefit from Linear Marginal Curves
questions.prompt_template: A workshop faces linear marginal benefit MB = 24 - 2Q and marginal cost MC = 4Q (in dollars per unit), with zero fixed cost. What is the optimal quantity Q* and the maximum total net benefit NB(Q*)?

hints.text: First solve MB = MC (24 - 2Q = 4Q) to find Q* and equilibrium marginal value.
Maximum net benefit equals the triangle area between MB (vertical intercept $24) and MC (origin $0) from Q = 0 to Q*: Area = 0.5 * base * height.

options_template.text: Q* = 4 units; Maximum Net Benefit = $48.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 24 - 2Q = 4Q gives 6Q = 24 => Q* = 4 (MB = MC = $16). Triangle area = 0.5 * ($24 - $0) * 4 = $48 (also verified by TB(4) - TC(4) = $80 - $32 = $48).

options_template.text: Q* = 4 units; Maximum Net Benefit = $64.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rectangle Area Error): $16 * 4 = $64 computes a rectangle at equilibrium value rather than the triangle between MB and MC.

options_template.text: Q* = 4 units; Maximum Net Benefit = $96.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Triangle Factor 1/2): $24 * 4 = $96 forgets the 1/2 factor in the triangle area formula.

options_template.text: Q* = 4 units; Maximum Net Benefit = $32.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Cost Area Substitution): 0.5 * $16 * 4 = $32 equals Total Cost under MC, not Net Benefit between MB and MC.

questions.title: Evaluating a Fare Increase Holding Gasoline Prices Constant
questions.prompt_template: A city's monthly transit ridership R (in thousands of rides) is modeled by R = 150 - 20F + 12G, where F is the subway fare ($) and G is the local gasoline price ($/gallon). Starting from F = $2.50 and G = $3.50, what is the new monthly ridership R2 and the ceteris paribus change Delta R if the fare rises to F = $3.25 while G remains fixed at $3.50?

hints.text: Compute baseline R1 at F = 2.50, G = 3.50, then compute R2 at F = 3.25, G = 3.50.
Check your change using Delta R = (-20) * Delta F = (-20) * (+0.75).

options_template.text: R2 = 122 thousand rides; Delta R = -20 thousand rides.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Step Slope Error): Subtracting 20 assumes a full $1.00 fare hike instead of the actual $0.75 increase (-20 * 0.75 = -15).

options_template.text: R2 = 127 thousand rides; Delta R = -15 thousand rides.
R2 = 157 thousand rides; Delta R = +15 thousand rides.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Adding 15 reverses the negative fare coefficient (-20), implying higher fares increase ridership.

options_template.text: R2 = 85 thousand rides; Delta R = -15 thousand rides.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dropped Held-Constant Term): 150 - 20(3.25) = 85 omits the +12(3.50) = +42 gasoline-price term from the intercept.

questions.title: Collapsing a Multivariable Model to Y = a + bX Under Ceteris Paribus
questions.prompt_template: In the chapter's transit ridership model R = 120 - 15F + 10G, suppose local gasoline prices are held constant at G = $4.50 per gallon. Which single-variable linear equation R = a + bF captures the relationship between fare F and ridership R?

hints.text: Substitute the fixed value G = 4.50 directly into the term +10G.
Combine the resulting constant with 120 to form the new vertical intercept a.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Fixed Variable): Holding G constant at $4.50 does not set G = 0; you must include +10(4.50) = +45 inside the intercept.
Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Sign Error): Subtracting 10(4.50) = 45 from 120 instead of adding it reverses the positive effect of gasoline prices on transit demand.
Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Sign Error): Although the intercept 165 is correct, the fare slope must remain -15, not +15.

questions.title: Decomposing Simultaneous Changes in Fare and Gas Prices
questions.prompt_template: Using the transit ridership model R = 120 - 15F + 10G (in thousands of rides), suppose the subway fare rises by $0.80 (Delta F = +0.80) during the same month that gasoline prices rise by $0.50 per gallon (Delta G = +0.50). What is the net change in monthly ridership (Delta R)?

hints.text: Compute each variable's separate effect: (-15 * Delta F) and (+10 * Delta G).
Add the two partial effects together: Delta R = -15(0.80) + 10(0.50).

options_template.text: -17 thousand rides (-17,000 rides).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gas-Effect Sign Reversal): Computing -12 - 5 = -17 treats higher gas prices as reducing transit ridership rather than encouraging drivers to switch to transit.

options_template.text: -12 thousand rides (-12,000 rides).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Secondary Shock): -15(0.80) = -12 accounts only for the fare hike and ignores the offsetting +5 thousand rides from higher gas prices.

options_template.text: -5 thousand rides (-5,000 rides).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Step Magnitudes): Adding the raw coefficients -15 + 10 = -5 assumes both variables rose by $1.00 instead of $0.80 and $0.50.

options_template.text: -7 thousand rides (-7,000 rides).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Delta R = -15(+0.80) + 10(+0.50) = -12 + 5 = -7 thousand rides (a net drop of 7,000 rides).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating College Enrollment During Economic Recessions
questions.prompt_template: The opportunity-cost model predicts that when entry-level wages fall during a recession, the opportunity cost of attending college full-time decreases, all else equal. Why does this NOT guarantee that college enrollment rises in every recession?

hints.text: Remember the meaning of ceteris paribus ('all else equal') in real-world recessions.
Consider other variables—such as household savings, credit access, or public university tuition—that may change simultaneously.

options_template.text: Because students never respond to changes in implicit opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Response Assertion): Empirical evidence shows opportunity costs do influence schooling choices; the issue is that other factors can move in the opposite direction.

options_template.text: Because other factors—such as declining family income, tighter borrowing constraints, or state tuition hikes—can simultaneously shift and offset the lower opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The opportunity-cost prediction holds ceteris paribus; in real recessions, lost family income or higher tuition can outweigh lower forgone wages.

options_template.text: Because explicit tuition costs become sunk costs as soon as a recession begins.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost Misapplication): Future tuition for an upcoming semester has not been paid yet and is still an avoidable explicit cost.

options_template.text: Because economic models apply only during economic expansions, never during recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Rejection): Economic principles apply across the business cycle, provided all shifting variables are accounted for.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Sunk Cost Fallacy in Public Policy
questions.title: Evaluating a Cost-Overrun Public Infrastructure Project
questions.prompt_template: A city has already spent $400 million constructing a transit tunnel that cannot be repurposed. Engineers now determine that finishing the tunnel requires an additional $300 million, while the completed tunnel will generate $200 million in total future public benefits. A council member argues, 'We must spend the $300 million so our $400 million is not wasted.' How should an economist evaluate this argument?

hints.text: Identify which dollar amounts are already unrecoverable versus which are incremental forward-looking costs and benefits.
Compare the future marginal benefit ($200M) against the future marginal cost ($300M).

options_template.text: It commits the sunk cost fallacy: the $400 million is gone either way, and spending $300 million more to gain $200 million loses an additional $100 million.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rational forward-looking evaluation compares incremental benefit ($200M) to incremental cost ($300M), showing the project should be halted.

options_template.text: It is economically sound because total benefits ($200M) plus sunk outlays ($400M) exceed the remaining $300 million cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Sunk Costs to Benefits): Already-spent money is a past cost, not a future benefit.

options_template.text: It is sound only if the city borrows the $300 million instead of raising taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financing Illusion): Borrowing does not eliminate the $300 million opportunity cost of resources used to finish the tunnel.

options_template.text: The city should finish the tunnel because stopping would reduce accounting profit to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Loss Aversion): Finishing turns a $400 million sunk loss into a $500 million total net loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Nuanced Interpretation of Seatbelt Mandates and the Peltzman Effect
questions.prompt_template: Following the January 1, 1968 U.S. federal seat-belt mandate, economist Sam Peltzman (1975) hypothesized that safer cars could induce some drivers to drive faster or more aggressively. Which conclusion accurately reflects the economic meaning of the Peltzman effect?

hints.text: Focus on how lower personal crash risk changes a driver's marginal cost of risky driving.
Carefully distinguish between an offsetting behavioral hypothesis and a universal claim about total fatalities.

options_template.text: Seat-belt laws are proven to increase total traffic fatalities in every country and should be repealed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overclaiming Hypothesis as Universal Law): The Peltzman effect is a hypothesis about offsetting incentives, not a claim that seat belts generally raise total deaths.

options_template.text: Drivers ignore safety equipment completely because driving habits are fixed by biology.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Incentive Response): Economics recognizes that people may adjust behavior when marginal risk costs change, with the exact size being an empirical question.

options_template.text: Lower perceived driver risk reduces the marginal cost of speeding, which may partially offset safety gains and shift risk toward people outside the vehicle—with net effects depending on empirical evidence.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Peltzman effect highlights potential risk compensation and risk shifting at the margin, while emphasizing that actual magnitudes depend on evidence and context.

options_template.text: Mandating seat belts raises the marginal cost of speeding, eliminating all pedestrian accidents.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Greater crash survivability lowers—not raises—the driver's personal marginal cost of risky driving.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Predicting Behavioral Responses to Perverse Policy Incentives
questions.prompt_template: To reduce municipal landfill waste, a city replaces a flat monthly trash fee with a $5-per-bag fee on curbside garbage bags while keeping recycling free and enforcement of illegal dumping minimal. Using marginal analysis, which unintended behavioral response should policymakers anticipate?

hints.text: Examine how the $5-per-bag fee raises the marginal cost of legal curbside disposal relative to alternative margins.
Think about both intended adjustments (recycling) and unintended margins (illegal dumping or stuffing non-recyclables into recycling bins).

options_template.text: Households will increase garbage generation because paying per bag creates a sunk cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost & Direction Error): A per-bag fee is an avoidable marginal cost ($5/bag), not a sunk cost, and it discourages—not encourages—legal bagging.

options_template.text: Household behavior will not change at all because trash disposal is a necessity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Elasticity Myth): Even for basic services, people adjust on multiple margins when marginal costs change.

options_template.text: Total recycling will fall because the marginal cost of legal trash bags rose.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Direction Error): Making legal trash costlier raises the relative attractiveness of free recycling.

options_template.text: While legal trash volume falls and recycling rises, some residents may respond to the higher marginal cost of legal bags by illegally dumping trash or contaminating free recycling bins.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rational agents optimize across all available margins; raising MC of legal disposal without enforcement can trigger substitution into illegal dumping or wish-cycling.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: When the Airline Standby Discount Rule Breaks Down
questions.prompt_template: In Section 1.2's Work It Out problem, an airline gains +$50 by selling an empty standby seat for $65 when incremental fuel/snack cost is $15. Under what real-world condition could routinely offering $65 last-minute standby fares actually REDUCE the airline's total profit?

hints.text: Recall the explicit simplifying assumption stated in the standby ticket problem.
What happens to the airline's implicit opportunity cost if passengers who would have paid $250 in advance start waiting for $65 standby seats?

options_template.text: If regular passengers who would have paid $250 in advance wait for $65 standby seats, creating an implicit cannibalization cost that makes true marginal cost exceed $65.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Cannibalizing full-fare bookings adds lost revenue to the true opportunity cost of the standby policy, violating the no-cannibalization assumption.

options_template.text: If the flight's $15,000 fixed operating cost rises to $20,000 before tickets go on sale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Irrelevance at Departure): Once the plane is scheduled to fly, higher committed fixed costs do not change the $15 incremental boarding cost.

options_template.text: If the standby fare ($65) remains below the airline's $100 average cost per seat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Cost Fallacy): Pricing below average cost still raises profit whenever MB exceeds true marginal cost (including any cannibalization).

options_template.text: If all 12 empty seats are filled at $65 each rather than just 1 empty seat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scale Reversal): Filling 12 otherwise-empty seats without cannibalization increases profit by 12 * $50 = +$600.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Disentangling Mixed Policy Statements on the Minimum Wage
questions.prompt_template: A legislator declares: 'Raising the city minimum wage from $16 to $20 will raise annual earnings for low-wage workers by 10%, so the city council has a moral duty to pass this bill immediately.' How should an economist dissect this statement?

hints.text: Break the sentence into its two clauses: the quantitative earnings prediction and the 'moral duty to pass' recommendation.
Match each clause to positive (testable) versus normative (value judgment) economics.

options_template.text: The entire statement is positive because it includes specific dollar and percentage numbers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Numbers-Make-It-Positive): Including numbers in the first clause does not make the 'moral duty' prescription in the second clause positive.

options_template.text: The first clause is a positive prediction testable with labor-market data, while the second clause is a normative value judgment that data alone cannot settle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Predicting a 10% earnings increase is a testable positive claim, whereas arguing the council has a moral duty to pass the bill is a normative judgment.

options_template.text: The entire statement is normative because minimum-wage legislation is decided by politicians.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domain-Based Misclassification): Politicians frequently make positive empirical claims alongside normative recommendations.

options_template.text: The first clause is normative because economists disagree about minimum-wage effects, while the second clause is positive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disagreement-Equals-Normative): Empirical disagreement over magnitudes makes a question an active positive research issue, not a normative one.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Ceteris Paribus Failure in Empirical Data
questions.title: Diagnosing a Confounded Fare-Hike Observation
questions.prompt_template: A city raises its subway fare from $2.00 to $3.00 in January. That same month, local gasoline prices surge from $4.00 to $5.50 per gallon, and observed monthly subway ridership stays unchanged at 130,000 rides. A transit official concludes: 'Subway riders do not care about fare hikes at all.' What flaw undermines this conclusion?

hints.text: Plug F = 3.00 and G = 5.50 into the chapter model R = 120 - 15F + 10G to see why ridership stayed at 130.
Ceteris paribus was violated because gasoline prices changed simultaneously in the opposite direction.

options_template.text: The official confused accounting cost with economic cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Concept): The error concerns isolating causal effects when multiple variables shift, not explicit versus implicit costs.

options_template.text: The official applied the sunk cost fallacy to past transit fares.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost Misattribution): Current subway fares are avoidable out-of-pocket costs for each trip, not sunk costs.

options_template.text: Ceteris paribus was violated: the $1.50 surge in gasoline prices boosted transit demand (+15,000 rides), masking the negative ridership effect (-15,000 rides) of the fare hike.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In R = 120 - 15F + 10G, raising F by $1 cuts ridership by 15,000 while raising G by $1.50 adds 15,000, leaving observed ridership flat even though riders do respond to fares.

options_template.text: Linear models cannot be used whenever two variables change in the same month.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model-Rejection Error): Multivariable models explicitly handle simultaneous changes once both variables are controlled for.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Using the Two-Sector Circular Flow Model Appropriately
questions.prompt_template: A policy analyst tries to use Figure 1.3's two-sector Circular Flow Diagram (households and firms only) to calculate how a new federal payroll tax affects national saving and imports. What is the most rigorous methodological critique of this approach?

hints.text: Recall the simplifying assumptions explicitly stated for Figure 1.3 in Section 1.3.
Determine whether the model is wrong in principle or simply needs to be extended to include the sectors relevant to the question.

options_template.text: The circular flow model is completely invalid and should never be taught in economics.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-or-Nothing Model Rejection): Simplified models are valid for their intended scope (core household–firm exchange) even if they must be extended for fiscal or trade policy.

options_template.text: The analyst can still answer the question because payroll taxes appear on the dashed inner loop of Figure 1.3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing-Sector Oversight): Figure 1.3 has no government, financial, or foreign sector on either loop.

options_template.text: Payroll taxes are purely normative and therefore cannot be represented in any economic diagram.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Positive/Normative Confusion): Analyzing how a tax changes saving and imports is a positive economic question.

options_template.text: Figure 1.3 intentionally abstracts away from government, financial markets, and international trade, so analyzing payroll taxes, saving, and imports requires extending the model to include those sectors.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every model's simplifying assumptions define its domain; answering fiscal, financial, and open-economy questions requires adding those sectors to the baseline map.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Matching Analytical Lenses to Housing Market Policies
questions.prompt_template: City officials want to evaluate two separate housing developments: (I) how a municipal up-zoning ordinance affects neighborhood apartment rents and individual households' buy-versus-rent choices, and (II) how a 2-percentage-point Federal Reserve interest-rate increase affects nationwide housing starts and U.S. GDP. How should economists assign these inquiries?

hints.text: Match local market / individual buyer decisions to microeconomics, and central-bank / national aggregate effects to macroeconomics.
Review Bring It Home: Separating Micro from Macro in Housing Policy.

options_template.text: Inquiry (I) is primarily microeconomic (local market prices and household choices), whereas Inquiry (II) is primarily macroeconomic (national monetary policy and aggregate output).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Microeconomics analyzes individual markets and buyer decisions, while macroeconomics examines Fed rate policy and nationwide aggregate construction/GDP.

options_template.text: Both inquiries are macroeconomic because housing is a major component of consumer budgets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Size-Equals-Macro Fallacy): Even large industries are studied microeconomically when examining individual market pricing, zoning, and buyer choices.

options_template.text: Both inquiries are microeconomic because Federal Reserve interest rates affect individual mortgage borrowers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Micro-Only Reductionism): Studying economy-wide Fed policy, national housing starts, and GDP belongs to macroeconomics.

options_template.text: Inquiry (I) is normative economics, whereas Inquiry (II) is positive economics.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope vs. Methodology Confusion): Both inquiries are framed as positive empirical questions ('how does X affect Y?').

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting Zero Economic Profit for a Business Owner
questions.prompt_template: After her second year running an independent design studio, Maya discovers that her accounting profit is $66,000 while her economic profit is exactly $0. Should Maya immediately shut down her studio because she is 'making nothing'?

hints.text: Recall what zero economic profit means when implicit costs include Maya's $65,000 forgone salary and $1,000 forgone savings interest.
Does economic profit = $0 mean zero income, or earning exactly as much as her next-best alternative?

options_template.text: Yes, because zero economic profit means Maya received $0 in take-home income and cannot pay her bills.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Income Misconception): Maya earned $66,000 in accounting profit—enough to fully compensate her time and capital.

options_template.text: No, because zero economic profit means her studio covers all explicit bills and earns exactly as much as her best alternative (her $65,000 salary plus $1,000 savings interest).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Zero economic profit ('normal profit') means the owner is doing just as well financially as in her next-best alternative career and investment.

options_template.text: Yes, because any business with zero economic profit must have negative accounting profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit-Order Inversion): Because implicit costs are positive, zero economic profit implies strictly positive accounting profit.

options_template.text: No, because she should keep operating regardless of losses to recover her Year-1 startup expenses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk Cost Fallacy): Past startup expenses are sunk; staying open is justified because current revenue covers current explicit and implicit costs, not because of past spending.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating 'Free' Campus Parking
