questions.prompt_template: A university advertises 'free campus parking' for commuters on a valuable downtown lot that does not charge a daily gate fee. Why do economists argue that this parking is NOT truly free?

hints.text: Distinguish between a $0 explicit checkout price and the real resources tied up in providing the parking lot.
Ask what else the university could have built on that downtown land (such as student housing or classrooms).

options_template.text: Because commuters still pay a sunk cost when they buy gasoline for their cars.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost Mislabeling): Gasoline burned to commute is an avoidable explicit travel cost, not the core reason the parking lot itself has an opportunity cost.

options_template.text: Because economic scarcity applies only to private businesses, not public universities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Public-Sector Exemption Myth): Public universities face tight land and budget constraints, making scarcity central to campus planning.

options_template.text: Because a $0 gate price hides real opportunity costs: the land, maintenance funds, and student fees used for parking could otherwise fund dormitories, scholarships, or classrooms.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even when explicit user fees are zero, scarce land and funding have positive implicit and explicit opportunity costs ('there is no such thing as a free lunch').

options_template.text: Because free parking guarantees that marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost for every driver.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency Guarantee): Zero user pricing typically encourages over-consumption and congestion where social MC exceeds MB.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Optimal Pollution Abatement Rarely Equals Zero Pollution
questions.prompt_template: A regional air-quality study finds that reducing factory soot emissions from 0% to 90% abatement generates $500 million in total health benefits at a total cost of $120 million. Eliminating the final 10% of emissions (from 90% to 100%) would add $25 million in health benefits but require $180 million in extra scrubbing technology. Using marginal analysis, how should policymakers evaluate pushing abatement from 90% to 100%?

hints.text: Compare the incremental benefit ($25M) and incremental cost ($180M) of the final 10% step rather than looking only at overall program totals.
Remember that even when total benefit exceeds total cost for the whole program (525M > 300M), a marginal step with MC > MB reduces net social welfare.

options_template.text: Approve the final 10% step because cumulative total benefits ($525M) still exceed cumulative total costs ($300M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-vs-Marginal Fallacy): Even though the overall program remains net positive ($225M), the final 10% step destroys $155M in net benefit compared to stopping at 90% ($380M).

options_template.text: Cancel the entire air-quality program because the final 10% step costs more than it benefits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-or-Nothing Fallacy): The first 90% abatement generates +$380M in net benefit; marginal analysis adjusts at the margin rather than scrapping the whole program.

options_template.text: Approve the final 10% step because the average cost per percent abated ($3M) is less than the average benefit ($5.25M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Value Fallacy): Favorable averages mask an incremental step whose marginal cost ($180M) is more than seven times its marginal benefit ($25M).

options_template.text: Reject the move from 90% to 100% abatement because its marginal cost ($180M) exceeds its marginal benefit ($25M), reducing net social benefit by $155M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Marginal analysis stops before an increment where MC ($180M) > MB ($25M); those $180M of resources could achieve far greater health gains elsewhere.
